1 .  The brief facts of the present case as averred in the plaint are that the plaintiff is the owner of the freehold property bearing No. BP-76, Shalimar Bagh, Delhi.

That the ground floor of the said property comprising of 1 living room, 2 Bedrooms, 1 Kitchen, 2 Toilets, front and Back Verandah,
(hereinafter referred as suit premises/ tenanted premises and specifically shown in red colour in the site plan attached herewith) was taken on rent @ Rs. 5,000/- per month excluding the electricity and water charge by the father of the defendant in June 1998 vide agreement dated 29.06.1998 for a period of 22 months.
However, the suit premises was not vacated after the expiry of the said tenancy period and thus, the tenancy continued for month to month basis, till the father of the defendant had expired.

2. That thereafter the defendant has approached the plaintiff to execute the rent agreement in the name of the defendant for the suit property on rent @ Rs. 6,000/- per month excluding the electricity and water charges.
The same was duly agreed by the plaintiff, and the rent agreement was executed on 01.09.2003 for the period of 11 months between the defendant and plaintiff.
3. That after the expiry of the 11 months the suit premises was not vacated by the defendant and the tenancy continued on month to month basis.
It is further stated that from November 2005 the rent was orally and mutually increased to Rs. 7,000/- per month excluding the electricity and water charges NEHA by NEHA MITTAL
MITTAL

Date: 2024.11.05 16:11:23 +0530 which has been duly deposited by the defendant till October, 2019 in the bank A/c No. 071200101770332 (Old No.) (New No.520101208739420) of the plaintiff maintained in Corporation Bank, Shalimar Bagh.

4. It is further stated that in end of September 2019, the plaintiff had personally approached the defendant at the tenanted premises with the request to vacate the tenanted premises which was agreed by the defendant in lieu of consideration of Rs. 1 lakh to be paid by the plaintiff and accordingly, the plaintiff paid the part amount of Rs. 50,000/- to the defendant, by issuing a self cheque in the name of wife of defendant namely Anju Gupta, through Cheque No. 585985, drawn on Corporation Bank, Shalimar Bagh, Delhi dated 13.11.2019, which was duly encashed.

It was agreed that the balance amount will be paid at the time of handing over the vacant physical peaceful possession of the tenanted premises to the plaintiff by the defendant but when the plaintiff approached the defendant on 28.11.2019, to inquire about the status of handing over the possession of the tenanted premises, he was shocked to hear the refusal of the defendant to vacate the tenanted premises and even threatened the plaintiff, to create third party interest in the tenanted premises by further handing over the possession to some land grabbers of the area.
5. Accordingly, the tenancy of the defendant was terminated by the plaintiff vide legal notice dated 30.11.2019 which was duly replied to by the defendant.

It is further stated NEHA Digitally signed by NEHA MITTAL MITTAL Date: 2024.11.05 16:11:30 +0530 that as the defendant has failed to handover the vacant and peaceful possession of the tenanted premises after termination of tenancy therefore the defendant is also liable to pay the damages to the tune of Rs. 1,000/- per day, since 20.12.2019.

Hence, the present suit has been filed with the following prayers:

The same being admitted by the defendant, the burden of proof upon the plaintiff to prove the said fact stands discharged.
19. The next question is what was the rate of rent at which the suit property was let out by the plaintiff to the defendant.

The case of the plaintiff is that the suit property was initially let out to the father of the defendant as a rate of Rs.

Perusal of record shows that both the parties are on the same page regarding the mode of payment of rent i.e. by way of deposit in the bank account of the plaintiff bearing no.
071200101770332.
The bank account statement Ex. PW1/4 (OSR) has been duly proved by the plaintiff by summoning PW2.

A reading of the said bank account statement shows that there are regular monthly deposit enteries of Rs. 6,000/- per month from 15.06.2004 till 06.10.2005 except for one deposit of Rs. 5,000/- in the month of September, 2005.

It is pertinent to note here that the plaintiff has claimed the rate of rent to be Rs. 6,000/- per month since the execution of rent agreement Ex. PW1/3 (OSR) and thus, prima facie it appears that the said deposit entries are towards the rent being tendered by the defendant with respect to the suit property.

The mere fact that the particulars of the deposit entry do not clearly show that the said deposits have been made by the defendant cannot tilt the case in favour of the defendant because there is no other deposit entry in the bank account of plaintiff during the aforesaid period.

Thus, even if the version of defendant that the said deposit entry is not towards the rent is NEHA by NEHA MITTAL MITTAL 16:12:58 Date: 2024.11.05 +0530 believed to be true, then, it is noteworthy that the defendant has failed to prove that as to how and when he tendered the rent of the suit property as the defendant has admitted in his written statement that the rent was being deposited by him in the said bank account of the plaintiff.
21. The plaintiff has averred that the rent was mutually and orally increased to Rs. 7,000/- per month from November, 2005.

The same also stands corroborated from the bank account statement Ex. PW1/4 (OSR) which shows a total deposit of Rs. 7,000/- per month in the bank account of the plaintiff from 16.11.2005 till October, 2019 except for a few months.

The mere fact of non-mentioning of the details of either the purpose of deposit of the said amount or the person who deposited the said amount under the head "Particulars" in the bank account statement cannot prejudice the case of the plaintiff as the defendant has failed to show any other deposit entry in the account statement which should otherwise have been there as rent is stated to have been deposited by the defendant in the bank account of the plaintiff.

22. The defendant has also argued that the court cannot look into the deposit slips Ex. PW1/6 (colly)
as permission of the court has not been sought to place them on record.

Though the said argument is indeed correct, but it is noteworthy that the said deposit slips were summoned by the plaintiff from the summoned witness PW2 and had the same been produced by him, they could have been relied upon by the court.

In the present case, the NEHA by NEHA MITTAL MITTAL Date:
2024.11.05 16:13:05 +0530 summoned witness PW2 has identified deposit slips Ex. PW1/6 (colly)
to have been issued by the concerned bank and thus, in the opinion of this court, the same can be looked into.
A perusal of the said deposit slips shows that deposit entries reflecting in the bank statement Ex. PW1/4 have been made by the LRs of deceased defendant.

23. Another relevant fact is that in reply to the legal notice sent by the defendant, the defendant has averred that the rate of rent was Rs. 2,000/- initially which was increased to Rs. 2,500/- in the year 2010 and Rs. 3,000/- in the year 2018.
However, in the written statement as well as evidence affidavit of the defendant, the defence of defendant is that the rent of the suit property has always been Rs. 3,000/-.
This self contradictory stand of the defendant has further weakened the case of the defendant.

Moreover, there are no correspond deposit entries to show the deposit of rent in the Pyare Lal Dwivedi vs Anju Gupta on 4 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76659407/

sentences.text: 24. The conduct of defendant can also be noticed from the fact that the rent of Rs. 3,000/- was deposited by him for the first time in December, 2019 i.e. after receiving the legal notice Ex. PW1/5.

26. In view of the above discussion, the plaintiff has discharged the onus of proof placed upon him.

sentences.text: As the legal notice Ex. PW-1/5 was duly replied by the defendant vide his reply dated 05.12.2019, the tenancy of the defendant is deemed to be terminated on receiving the legal notice.
Now, it is to be examined as to at what rate, mesne profits shall be awarded to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff has claimed mesne profits at the rate of Rs.1,000/- per day.
The plaintiff should have produced the evidence to prove that Rs.1,000/- per day would have been reasonable compensation for his deprivation of possession of the suit property by the defendant.
The plaintiff has produced the copy of rent agreement Mark B which pertains to some other property situated in the same area where the suit property is located.
However, as the original said document has not been produced on record, it cannot be said to have been duly proved in accordance with law.
In the absence of any evidence, the Court can take judicial notice that there had been steep rise in the rent of the properties in Delhi.

The Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Vinod Khanna v. Bakshi Sachdev (Deceased) through LRs, AIR 1996 Delhi 32, has held that :
"21.
[I]t is true that no substantial evidence has been led by the plaintiffs in respect of the increase of rent in the properties like that of the suit property.

However, it is a well known fact that the Digitally signed NEHA by NEHA MITTAL MITTAL Date:
2024.11.05 16:15:17 +0530 amount of rent for various properties in and around Delhi has been rising staggeringly and we cannot see why such judicial notice could not be taken of the fact about such increase of rents in the premises in and around Delhi which is a city of growing importance being the capital of the country which is a matter of public history.
At this stage we may appropriately refer to the Court taking judicial notice of the increase of price of land rapidly in the urban areas in connection with the land acquisition matters.

Even the Apex Court has taken judicial notice of the fact of universal escalation of rent and even raised rent of disputed premises by taking such judicial notice in case of D.C. Oswal v. V.K. Subbiah, AIR 1992 SC 184 :
1992(1) RCR 326(SC). 22.

entities.text:
D.C. Oswal v. V.K. Subbiah, AIR 1992 SC 184 :
1992(1) RCR 326(SC)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In that view of the matter we have no hesitation in our mind in holding that the trial court did not commit any illegality in taking judicial notice of the fact of increase of rents and determining the compensation in respect of the suit premises at Rs.10,000/- per month w.e.f. 19.1.1989, in view of the fact that the rent fixed for the said premises was at Rs. 6,000/- per month as far back as in the year 1974."
31.

Hence, considering the above said legal position in the present case, the Court is of the view that the plaintiff is entitled to mesne profits at rate of Rs.15,000 per month from 20.12.2019 till the handing over of the suit property by the defendant to plaintiff.

Whether the present petition is barred by section 50 of the DRC Act?
The burden to prove this issue is upon the defendant.

The plaintiff has produced the copy of rent agreement Mark B which pertains to some other property situated in the same area where the suit property is located.
However, as the original said document has not been produced on record, it cannot be said to have been duly proved in accordance with law.
In the absence of any evidence, the Court can take judicial notice that there had been steep rise in the rent of the properties in Delhi.
Hence, considering the above said legal position in the present case, the Court is of the view that the plaintiff is entitled to mesne profits at rate of Rs.15,000 per month from 20.12.2019 till the handing over of the suit property by the defendant to plaintiff.
